Glossary

    DevOps practices

    Words: 1249

    Bash in delivery pipelines: builds, environments, deployments and rollbacks, pre-merge checks, and secret handling. Plus the warning signs that a pipeline has outgrown shell scripts.

    Key idea of this page #

    In the delivery pipeline, Bash is used most frequently and mistakes cost the most, because a CI step is your script executed by an external runner: with someone else's flags, in a fresh process, and in a reset directory. Hence the first rule: every step must be self-contained, and non-trivial logic should live in a repository script that can be run locally. The second rule governs builds: version strings come from version control, and latest is not a version because you cannot roll back to it. The third: one script across all environments with a mandatory environment argument, because defaults eventually trigger accidental deployments to production. And the fourth, most common interview topic: design the rollback before writing the deployment.

    1 · Bash in pipelines: whose process is this? #

    A CI step is your script run by someone else's runner. Three facts about this execution define nearly all its behavior.

    # 1. runner sets flags, not you
#    without shell: -> bash -e
#    shell: bash -> + pipefail
set -euo pipefail   # -u is yours alone

# 2. each step is a new process
echo "VER=$v" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"

# 3. working directory is reset
cd "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE"

    Every CI pipeline step must be self-contained: it never relies on export from prior steps, never assumes a default directory, and declares its own strict mode explicitly. Extract complex logic into a dedicated .sh script in the repository: it can be executed locally, validated with shellcheck, and clearly reviewed in diffs - unlike dozens of lines embedded inside YAML.

    What gets asked: “Why is a variable set in one CI step invisible in the next, and how do you pass data between steps?”

    2 · Building artifacts: reproducibility over speed #

    A build script answers a single question: will tomorrow's build produce the exact same artifact as today's? Everything else is secondary.

    ver=$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)
sha=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

docker build \
  --build-arg VER="$ver" \
  -t "app:$sha" .

# artifact is named by version,
# never latest

    Reproducibility of build artifacts rests on three fundamental rules. Version strings must come directly from Git rather than manual variables that can be forgotten. The latest tag is not a version: rolling back to it reliably is impossible. The --dirty suffix immediately warns of an uncommitted working tree whose build artifact cannot be reproduced from Git history.

    What gets asked: “Where should artifact versions originate, and why is deploying latest prohibited?”

    3 · Environments Dev → QA → Prod: one script, distinct parameters #

    A classic anti-pattern is maintaining three similar scripts, one per environment. Within a month they diverge, and a production deployment no longer mirrors what was tested on QA.

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
env="${1:?dev|qa|prod}"
cfg="deploy/$env.env"
[ -f "$cfg" ] || { echo "missing $cfg" >&2; exit 2; }
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "$cfg"

[ "$env" = prod ] && : "${APPROVED:?confirmation required}"

    One script, external configuration, mandatory environment argument. Never provide default values for the target environment: a script defaulting to production without arguments will eventually deploy to production by accident. Gate production deployments behind an explicit approval variable, not an easily ignored file header comment.

    What gets asked: “How does a single script serve three environments, and how do you guard production from accidental execution?”

    4 · Deployment and rollback: design rollback first #

    The question asked more frequently in interviews than deployment itself: how do you roll back? If the answer requires a new build, it is the wrong answer.

    # releases side by side, current is a symlink
ln -sfn "/opt/app/rel/$ver" /opt/app/next
mv -T /opt/app/next /opt/app/current
systemctl reload app

# rollback = identical step targeting previous version

    Combining ln -sfn with mv -T provides an atomic cutover: at any instant, the symlink points either to the old release or the new release, with no intermediate state. A naive rm symlink && ln -s lacks this guarantee: between the two commands, the symlink does not exist at all.

    Post-deployment validation belongs in the script as well: querying /health with a bounded retry loop and triggering an automated rollback to the previous release if health checks fail.

    What gets asked: “How do you make release symlink switching atomic, and how is automated rollback structured?”

    5 · Pipeline quality: pre-merge checks #

    Linting shell scripts is just as vital a CI stage as application unit tests. It takes seconds and catches bugs that would otherwise surface in production.

    - run: |
    shopt -s globstar
    shellcheck **/*.sh
- run: shfmt -d -i 2 .
- run: bats tests/

    Run the script quality verification suite locally via pre-commit hooks so defect-laden code never reaches CI. Local developer checks and CI gate steps must execute the exact same command - otherwise teams suffer from “works on my machine, fails in CI” syndrome, destroying trust in the automated checks.

    What gets asked: “Which shell code checks do you include in CI pipelines, and why must they match local hooks?”

    6 · Secrets and CI logs #

    CI logs are visible to anyone with repository access and persist far longer than memory of the secret.

    # no:
set -x               # prints everything
echo "token=$TOKEN"
curl -u "u:$PASS" …  # visible in ps

# yes:
curl --netrc-file "$f" …
printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | cmd --token-stdin

    Handling secrets securely in scripts and CI pipelines rests on three rules. Never pass secrets as command-line arguments - process arguments are visible in ps to any local user; transmit them via stdin, files, or environment variables. Shell execution tracing via set -x is strictly forbidden in steps handling secrets. CI log masking provides no absolute guarantee: it matches exact strings only, so multi-line or re-encoded secrets will leak into build logs unmasked.

    What gets asked: “Why must passwords never be passed as command-line arguments, and what are the limits of CI secret masking?”

    7 · When a pipeline outgrows shell scripts #

    Signs that logic should move out of shell scripts:

    • the script manages state that must persist between invocations;
    • steps have non-linear dependencies - suited for Make or a CI DAG rather than a linear sequence;
    • identical logic is duplicated across three pipelines;
    • understanding the script requires knowing runner-specific CI environment variables.

    State calls for dedicated state management tools; non-linear workflows call for dependency graphs; duplication calls for shared repository scripts or custom CI actions; and runner coupling calls for extracting logic into standalone scripts runnable locally with identical arguments.

    And the converse: a fifteen-line Bash pipeline made readable by three comments does not need to become a custom plugin. The complexity of the tooling must be justified by the complexity of the problem, not its importance.

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Understanding that a CI step is an external execution of your code. Your time was well spent if you stopped being puzzled by differing behavior in CI and started checking: what flags were passed, which process executed it, and where the working directory points. That is the essence of rewiring: the pipeline stops being a black box and becomes a transparent environment running your own commands.

    1. Three facts about CI steps: runner-defined flags, fresh processes, reset working directory.
    2. Git-derived versions and the absolute prohibition of latest in deployments.
    3. One script across three environments with a mandatory environment argument and production gates.
    4. Atomic cutover via ln -sfn and mv -T, and rolling back with the exact same step.
    5. Pre-merge verification identical to local developer tooling.
    6. Secret security rules: never in arguments, no execution tracing, masking is not infallible.
    7. Indicators that a pipeline has outgrown shell, and the appropriate remedy for each.
